prompt: Assess the causal claim using the sources of endogeneity and propose how FitLoop could test it.
modelAnswer: Reverse causation: users who are already motivated and loyal are the ones who join challenges. Omitted variable: intrinsic motivation, fitness level or free time drives both challenge participation and retention. Selection / survivorship bias: the sample includes only users still subscribed after 12 months – those who cancelled are missing. Measurement: what counts as “joining” a challenge? Test: a randomized experiment – randomly invite half of new users to challenges (A/B test) and compare cancellation rates.

prompt: Identify at least four biases with the Kahneman, Lovallo & Sibony checklist and propose remedies.
modelAnswer: Self-interest bias: bonuses of the deal team depend on closing → review with extra care. Saliency bias: one memorable 2015 analogy → ask for several comparable deals incl. failures (reference class). Anchoring / over-optimism: 25 % synergies from one case, single scenario → independent estimates, outside view, worst case. Groupthink: CEO states view first, no dissent → silence the leader, solicit dissent privately, red team. Possibly disaster neglect → premortem. Also the affect heuristic (CEO in love with the deal).

prompt: Which biases related to expertise and information filtering are at work, and how could the company counter them?
modelAnswer: Einstellung effect / cognitive entrenchment: her expertise makes her prioritize the known solution (better printed guides) over new, more appropriate ones. Confirmation bias: she relies on past evidence that fits her belief (“we have always seen that”) – selective exposure and retention. Possibly in-group favoritism (experts vs “strangers”) and dichotomous thinking (experts OR users). Countermeasures: bring in outside views and data on traveller behaviour, assign a red team to build the app case, run a small experiment, ask what a newcomer CEO would do.
